title: Multiprotocol Label Switching Architecture
summary: Describes the architecture of Multiprotocol Label Switching, where routers forward packets using short labels instead of examining full IP destination addresses at every hop. It explains label switched paths and the roles of routers. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS forwards packets by using short labels instead of re-reading full IP addresses at every hop. A router at the edge of the network puts a label on each packet; later routers look up that label to decide where to send the packet next.

questions: what is a forwarding equivalence class
what is an mpls label stack
what is a label switched path
subtitle: How routers forward packets by swapping short labels instead of re-reading IP addresses at every hop.

tldr.problem: In conventional IP forwarding, every router analyzes each packet's header to choose the next hop, even when that choice could be made once.
tldr.mechanism: MPLS assigns each packet to a forwarding equivalence class when it enters the network and encodes that class as a short label; later routers forward by swapping labels.
tldr.outcome: This architecture defines label switched paths, label distribution, and the rules for forwarding with label stacks. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 6178 and RFC 6790.

today: RFC 3031 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 6178 and RFC 6790.

sections.title: Why Forward by Label
sections.content:
RFC 3031 defines the architecture for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS). In conventional IP forwarding, each router analyzes the packet's header and runs a routing algorithm to choose the next hop. The document splits this into two functions: sorting packets into Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs), and mapping each FEC to a next hop.

In MPLS, a packet is assigned to a FEC only once, when it enters the network. That FEC is encoded as a short fixed length value called a label, which travels with the packet. At later hops, routers use the label as an index into a table that gives the next hop and a new label; the old label is replaced and the packet is forwarded. A router that supports MPLS is a Label Switching Router (LSR).
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS does the address work once at the edge of the network. The edge router puts a small label on the packet. Every router after that reads only the label to decide where to send the packet.

sections.title: Labels, Bindings and Label Distribution
sections.content:
A label is a short, fixed length identifier for a FEC. It is not an encoding of the network address. When upstream LSR Ru sends a packet to downstream LSR Rd, Ru labels the packet with value L if and only if the packet belongs to FEC F. That is a binding between L and F; the meaning of L is local to Ru and Rd.

Bindings are made by the downstream LSR and distributed to the upstream LSR (downstream-assigned). A label distribution protocol carries these bindings between label distribution peers. Distribution may be downstream-on-demand (asked for) or unsolicited downstream (sent without being asked). A binding may be kept by a peer even if it is not the next hop (Liberal Label Retention) or discarded (Conservative Label Retention).
sections.plainLanguage: A label is a small tag that means something only between two neighboring routers. The router closer to the destination picks the tag and tells the router behind it what the tag means.

sections.title: Forwarding Tables
sections.content:
A packet may carry more than one label in a label stack, processed last-in, first-out using the top label. Three structures control forwarding: the Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry (NHLFE), the Incoming Label Map (ILM), and the FEC-to-NHLFE Map (FTN).

The NHLFE gives the packet's next hop and an operation on the label stack: replace the top label with a new one, pop the stack, or replace the top label and push one or more labels. The ILM maps each incoming label to a set of NHLFEs for labeled packets. The FTN maps each FEC to a set of NHLFEs for unlabeled packets that are to be labeled. When a set has more than one entry, exactly one is chosen for forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router keeps a table that says: for this label, send the packet to this next router and put this new label on it. For packets with no label, the router looks up the destination class and picks a label to put on.

sections.title: Label Switched Paths and Tunnels
sections.content:
A Label Switched Path (LSP) is the sequence of routers a packet follows while being switched on a label at a given level. It starts at the LSP ingress, which pushes a label, and ends at the LSP egress, where a decision is made on a lower-level label or by ordinary forwarding. Multiple LSPs for the same FEC from different ingresses that share an egress form a multipoint-to-point tree.

With penultimate hop popping, the next-to-last router removes the label so the egress does one lookup instead of two. The penultimate router does this only if the egress requests it or if the next hop does not support MPLS. An LSP tunnel lets a router send packets to another router that is not the normal next hop; tunnels can nest because of the label stack.
sections.plainLanguage: An LSP is the path a packet takes while following its label. Sometimes the label comes off one hop before the end to make things simpler. A tunnel lets packets travel along a special path inside the network, using an extra label.

sections.title: Invalid Labels and TTL
sections.content:
If an LSR receives a labeled packet whose incoming label has no binding, the packet MUST be discarded unless it can be shown that forwarding it unlabeled is harmless. If the label is valid but the ILM gives no outgoing entry, the same rule applies.

For Time To Live (TTL), a packet leaving an LSP SHOULD have the TTL it would have had without label switching. If labels are carried in a shim header, that header MUST have a TTL field that SHOULD be loaded from the network header, decremented at each hop, and copied back at the end of the LSP. For a non-TTL LSP segment (where hardware cannot decrement TTL), the packet SHOULD still emerge with the correct TTL, and if it would expire inside the segment, the ingress SHOULD NOT label switch it.
sections.plainLanguage: If a router sees a label it does not know, it should discard the packet rather than guess. MPLS also keeps track of how many hops a packet has traveled, so packets that would loop too long do not circulate forever.

sections.title: Label Encoding and Merging
sections.content:
Labels may be carried in a protocol-independent shim between the data link and network layer headers (defined in RFC 3032), or in ATM cell headers in different encodings. Hops of one LSP may use different encodings, but successive ATM switches must use the same one.

Label merging means sending packets of one FEC that arrived with different labels or on different interfaces out with a single label. ATM switches using some encodings cannot merge because of cell interleaving; methods exist (VP merge, VC merge) when possible. MPLS supports both merging and non-merging LSRs. The choice affects how labels are distributed and how many labels are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: There is more than one way to carry the label with a packet. Merging means several incoming streams for the same destination can share one outgoing label, which reduces the number of labels a router must keep track of.

sections.title: Label Distribution Procedures
sections.content:
With independent LSP control, each LSR binds labels and tells peers on its own. With ordered LSP control, an LSR binds a label only if it is the egress or has already received a binding from its next hop. Ordered control is needed when traffic must follow specified properties; the two modes interoperate.

The RFC defines procedures and supported combinations (schemes). For LSRs that support label merging, 7 schemes are defined; for LSRs that do not support label merging, 3 schemes are defined. Route selection can be hop-by-hop or explicit (strict or loose). Aggregation (binding one label to a union of FECs) reduces label counts and control traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers need rules for offering labels, asking for them, and when to forget old ones. The rules differ depending on whether routers can merge streams together and whether they set up paths in order from end to start.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes two security points. First, inserting the MPLS shim between the data link header and network layer header may break security procedures that depend on the network layer header being at a fixed position relative to the data link header.

Second, a label's meaning comes only from agreement between the LSR that writes it and the LSR that reads it. If labeled packets are accepted from untrusted sources, or if an incoming label is accepted from an LSR to which that label was not distributed, packets may be routed in an illegitimate manner.
sections.plainLanguage: A label only works because two routers agreed on what it means. If a router accepts labels from an untrusted source, packets could be sent to the wrong place.

left.title: Conventional IP forwarding
left.desc: Each router analyzes the packet header and chooses the next hop independently.

right.title: MPLS forwarding
right.desc: The packet gets a label once at entry; later routers forward by looking up and swapping the label.

items.title: NHLFE
items.text: Gives the next hop and an operation on the label stack (replace, pop, or replace and push).

items.title: ILM
items.text: Maps an incoming label to NHLFEs for packets that arrive labeled.

items.title: FTN
items.text: Maps a FEC to NHLFEs for packets that arrive unlabeled and need to be labeled.
